chunks: Techniques to reduce image noise. The question: What are some techniques to reduce image noise?
Image noise is the random grain in a photo. It has different sources, and each needs a different fix.
You can collect more light, make the electronics quieter, calibrate away patterns that repeat every frame, or smooth the picture in software.
Software smoothing is the last resort, because it can wipe out real detail.
Imagine talking to a friend at a loud party. You can get closer or speak up, which is like collecting more light.
You can step away from the speakers, which is like quieter electronics.
A steady hum from a fridge is the same every second, so you can learn it and mentally subtract it, like calibration.
Last, your brain guesses muffled words, like software denoising, and sometimes guesses wrong.
The party picture is loose about the hum: only noise that repeats exactly can be subtracted.
At low signal the read-noise floor (gray) dominates; in the middle, shot noise rises with slope 1/2 (green); at high signal PRNU (red, slope 1) takes over.

A fix that targets the wrong regime does nothing: bigger aperture helps the middle region, CDS and DCG lower the floor, flat-fielding lowers the red line, and stacking cannot touch the red line at all.
Shot noise: random variation in how many photons land on a pixel. Only more light reduces it. Read noise: electronic noise added each time the sensor is read out.
Dark current: unwanted electrons made by heat, even with no light. Fixed-pattern noise: pixel-to-pixel differences that are identical in every frame, such as a hot pixel.
Binning: combining neighboring pixels into one bigger pixel to gain signal.
Say each frame has random noise of 8 counts, and one hot pixel reads 10 counts too high in every frame. Average 4 frames.
The random noise drops to 4, because it shrinks by the square root of the number of frames. The hot pixel still reads 10 too high, since it is the same every time.
To fix that, take pictures with the lens capped, average them into a dark frame, and subtract it from your photos. That is the whole idea: match each fix to its noise source.
"I group it into three: more signal, quieter electronics, and cleanup.
For signal, shot noise dominates so use more photons: wider aperture, longer exposure, bigger pixels or binning, and frame stacking, which gives root N.
For electronics: low-read-noise sensor with correlated double sampling, clean analog supply, low gain, cooling.
For fixed patterns, calibrate with dark frames, flat fields and a defect map. Then denoise in the ISP with spatial, temporal or learned filters, accepting a detail trade-off."
Quick check. Which noise source is NOT reduced by averaging many frames?
